profile.summary: PepSpecBench is a benchmark for predicting peptide tandem mass spectra: given a modified peptide sequence, a precursor charge and a normalised collision energy, a model must predict the fragment-ion intensity pattern. It harmonises two public spectral libraries, PROSPECT and MassIVE-KB, into matched 500k/50k/50k train, validation and test subsets under one scope (peptide length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6, three PTMs), splits them so that no peptide backbone appears in two partitions, and projects every model's output into one 234-dimensional canonical ion space so that architectures with different native outputs can be compared. It adds a seven-subset cross-species suite of 20k spectra each, evaluated zero-shot, and metadata perturbation probes. Six models were retrained by the authors on these splits.

summary_quotes.text: enforces a strict backbone-disjoint splitting strategy to eliminate sequence leakage
PepSpecBench restricts evaluation to peptides of length L ∈ [6, 40], precursor charge z ∈ [1, 6], and three common PTMs (acetylation, carbamidomethylation, and oxidation)
Both sources are normalized to the shared physical scope and reconstructed into standardized 500k/50k/50k train/validation/test subsets.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a model reproduces the measured fragment-intensity pattern of a peptide's MS/MS spectrum, and how far that ability survives three stresses. First, fair comparison: all models are scored in one canonical ion space rather than in their own output formats. Second, leakage: whether apparent accuracy depends on seeing the same peptide backbone in training, tested by comparing three split rules under one model and one data source. Third, robustness: whether a model trained on human libraries transfers zero-shot to other species and to a cancer cell line, and whether it uses collision energy and precursor charge in a physically sensible way, probed by perturbing that metadata.

quotes.text: It further introduces a comprehensive multi-species evaluation suite and physically grounded metadata perturbation probes to assess model robustness and instrument awareness.

Our experiments show that naive random splits overestimate generalization, in-domain leaderboards do not reliably predict cross-species robustness, and high aggregate accuracy does not guarantee physically grounded use of collision energy or precursor charge.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Two in-domain sources are combined under one scope: PROSPECT, a curated spectral library with broad PTM coverage and several collision energies per peptide, and MassIVE-KB, a larger community-curated human library. Both are filtered to peptides of length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6 and the UNIMOD 1, 4 and 35 modifications, and reconstructed into 500k train, 50k validation and 50k test spectra each; the appendix names these PROSPECT-Mini and MassIVE-KB-Mini. Because MassIVE-KB mixes heterogeneous sources, a single default normalised collision energy of 25 is applied to all its spectra. The cross-species suite is seven subsets drawn from ProteomeXchange studies, each truncated to 20k spectra after the same filtering, covering human reference and HeLa, yeast, two E. coli subsets, C. elegans and A. thaliana, identified with MaxQuant at 1 per cent false discovery rate.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an intensity prediction for an input triplet of modified sequence, precursor charge and normalised collision energy. Because the six baselines have different native output spaces, each has a projection into one shared canonical ion space that enumerates every combination of cleavage position, b or y ion type and fragment charge up to a maximum; with a reference length of 40 and maximum fragment charge 3 this space has 234 dimensions. Prediction and ground truth are both projected, a validity mask is built, and three metrics are computed over the masked positions: spectral angle (SA), where lower is better and the range is 0 to 1, spectral angle similarity (1 minus SA), and Pearson correlation. Results are aggregated as medians with bootstrap confidence intervals. All six baselines were retrained by the authors on the benchmark splits.

quotes.text: In the present benchmark, Lref = 40 and zfrag = 3, yielding dim(C) = 234.
where SA ∈ [0, 1] and lower is better. Spectral Angle Similarity (SAS) = 1 − SA.

sections.title: The split rule and what it is worth
sections.body: A partition is backbone-disjoint when the sets of unmodified amino-acid sequences in any two partitions are mutually exclusive, which blocks both exact sequence reuse and the same backbone appearing with different modifications. PROSPECT is split by deterministic hashing of the backbone; for MassIVE-KB the official disjoint splits are kept, filtered within each partition, and checked for zero backbone overlap. The benefit is measured rather than asserted: with Prosit and PROSPECT held fixed, a naive random split lowers median SA from 0.1376 to 0.1254 and raises Pearson correlation from 0.8921 to 0.9099, while a modified-sequence split stays close to backbone-disjoint (SA 0.1392, correlation 0.8895). The authors read this as exact backbone reuse being the dominant leakage path, and state in their limitations that backbone disjointness does not remove higher-order sequence homology.

quotes.text: A partition {Dtrain , Dval , Dtest } is Backbone-Disjoint if the backbone sets of any two partitions are mutually exclusive. This blocks both exact-sequence reuse and PTM-variant overlap across splits.
For PROSPECT, we enforce backbone disjointness by deterministic hashing of the peptide backbone into train/validation/test partitions. For MassIVE-KB, we preserve the official disjoint splits
Naive random splitting inflates apparent accuracy. It artificially reduces median SA from 0.1376 (under Backbone-Disjoint) to 0.1254 and increases PCC from 0.8921 to 0.9099.
Although backbone-disjoint splitting removes backbone overlap, it does not eliminate all higher-order sequence homology, motivating future homology-aware partitioning.

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: The in-domain ranking depends on the source: Prosit Transformer has the best median SA on MassIVE-KB (0.0977 against 0.0995 for Prosit), while Prosit leads on PROSPECT (0.1376 against 0.1419), which the authors attribute to MassIVE-KB holding longer peptides and higher charges. Mid-tier models are less stable: UniSpec beats PredFull on PROSPECT but collapses on MassIVE-KB to SA 0.3369 with near-zero correlation, while PredFull holds at SA 0.1673. The in-domain ranking does not survive transfer: under MassIVE-KB training, PredFull beats both Prosit models on all five out-of-distribution testbeds, and the appendix shows the Prosit models reaching negative median correlation on several subsets. Under PROSPECT training the picture splits again, with Prosit best on C. elegans and A. thaliana and PredFull on E. coli and yeast. The authors note that one apparent out-of-distribution advantage is a Simpson's paradox caused by covariate shift.

quotes.text: On PROSPECT, the top ranking flips: Prosit leads with SA 0.1376, ahead of Prosit Transformer (0.1419) by 0.0043.

sections.title: How to get the data
sections.body: The dataset is published on Hugging Face under the MIT licence, with a dataset DOI. Its configurations mirror the benchmark components: massive_kb and prospect, each in a native representation with the original mass-to-charge and intensity arrays and in the canonical 234-dimensional representation, each with train, validation and test splits; an ood configuration in both representations with a test split only; and a small sample configuration. No evaluation code, model code or leaderboard address is given in the paper.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two in-domain components of 500k train, 50k validation and 50k test spectra each: PROSPECT-Mini, from ProteomeTools, balanced 50 per cent unmodified and 50 per cent modified in every split, and MassIVE-KB-Mini, from the MassIVE-KB v1 human subset at its natural modification rate (unmodified 75.40, 72.83 and 72.09 per cent in train, validation and test). Plus PepSpecBench-OOD, seven subsets of 20k spectra each: human reference, human HeLa, yeast, E. coli reference, E. coli enriched, C. elegans and A. thaliana. All components share the same length, charge and PTM scope.

(2) MassIVE-KB-Mini: 500k/50k/50k from MassIVE-KB v1 human subset, natural PTM distribution. (3) PepSpecBench-OOD: 7 subsets × 20k spectra covering five species (human, yeast, E. coli, C. elegans, A. thaliana).

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Backbone-disjoint train, validation and test splits for both in-domain sources: the unmodified amino-acid backbone sets of any two partitions are mutually exclusive, so neither an exact sequence nor another modified form of it can cross the boundary. PROSPECT is partitioned by deterministic hashing of the backbone; MassIVE-KB keeps its official disjoint splits, scope-filtered within each partition and verified to have zero backbone overlap. The seven cross-species subsets are test-only and used zero-shot. Two weaker rules, a naive random split and a modified-sequence split, are run as a controlled ablation for comparison.

quotes.text: A partition {Dtrain , Dval , Dtest } is Backbone-Disjoint if the backbone sets of any two partitions are mutually exclusive.
For PROSPECT, we enforce backbone disjointness by deterministic hashing of the peptide backbone into train/validation/test partitions. For MassIVE-KB, we preserve the official disjoint splits
All cross-species evaluation is conducted in a zero-shot setting: models are trained exclusively on in-domain data and evaluated on cross-species subsets without any fine-tuning or adaptation.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three metrics over the masked positions of the canonical space, the same for every task. Spectral angle (SA) is the primary one: the angular distance between the normalised predicted and observed intensity vectors, in the range 0 to 1, and lower is better. Spectral angle similarity is 1 minus SA, so higher is better. Pearson correlation measures whether relative intensity rankings are preserved, higher being better. All values are reported as medians with bootstrap confidence intervals.

quotes.text: where SA ∈ [0, 1] and lower is better. Spectral Angle Similarity (SAS) = 1 − SA.
PCC captures whether relative intensity rankings are preserved, complementing the angular geometry measured by SA.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Six models, all retrained by the authors on the benchmark splits. Sequence-centric, predicting b and y ion intensities by cleavage position and fragment charge: Prosit (GRU encoder-decoder, about 2.5M parameters), Prosit Transformer (about 86M) and AlphaPeptDeep (modular Transformer, about 1.8M). Full-spectrum or dictionary models projected into the canonical space: PredFull (residual CNN with squeeze-excitation, about 8.2M) and UniSpec (attention-based dictionary model, about 12M). FastSpel, a linear model of about 50K parameters, serves as a lower-bound reference.

quotes.text: We integrate six representative baselines that span the principal architectural families in MS/MS prediction.
Lightweight: FastSpel [3] (∼50K parameters) is a linear model whose output is projected to the canonical layout, serving as a lower-bound reference.
All baselines are retrained on the benchmark data under the Backbone-Disjoint splits described above.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The backbone-disjoint split is the benchmark's central control: no unmodified peptide backbone may appear in two partitions, which blocks exact reuse and PTM-variant overlap. Its effect is quantified by the split ablation, and residual similarity is measured in the appendix as the minimum Levenshtein edit distance from each test backbone to the nearest training backbone. The authors state the limit plainly: backbone disjointness does not eliminate higher-order sequence homology, and their own biases note says the backbone split does not eliminate homology-level leakage. Cross-species evaluation is an additional, stronger control, since those subsets come from different organisms and are used zero-shot.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Three things and no more: the modified peptide sequence, the precursor charge state and the normalised collision energy. No structure, alignment or spectrum is given at prediction time. The benchmark restricts the scope to peptide length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6 and the UNIMOD 1, 4 and 35 modifications, and a model's output may be in its own native format as long as a projection into the canonical space is defined.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training from scratch on the benchmark's own training split: all six baselines are retrained on the benchmark data under the backbone-disjoint splits, separately for each in-domain source, with per-model adaptations and hyperparameters documented in the appendix. The cross-species evaluation is strictly zero-shot, with no fine-tuning or adaptation on the out-of-distribution subsets.

strengths.text: The shared 234-dimensional canonical ion space lets models with different native outputs, from sequence-indexed ion ladders to binned full spectra and fragment dictionaries, be scored on the same footing, and every metric is computed only in that space.

strengths.text: The value of the strict split is measured rather than asserted: with the model and data source held fixed, a naive random split is shown to flatter the model by 0.012 median SA, while a modified-sequence split is shown to make little difference.
